summary: Gives guidelines for writing the IANA Considerations section of RFCs, so IANA knows how to manage the registries of constants and other values a protocol uses. It defines policies for how new values may be assigned. It replaces RFC 2434, is a Best Current Practice, and was replaced by RFC 8126.

eli5.summary: Many rules need numbered lists. This guide tells writers how to ask a record-keeper to hand out those numbers fairly.

questions: how to write an iana considerations section
what is an iana considerations section
how to choose iana registration policy
subtitle: Guidelines for writing the part of an RFC that tells IANA how to manage numbered registries.

tldr.problem: Protocols assign numbers to things like message types or options, but without clear guidelines, RFC authors and IANA cannot coordinate how new numbers are assigned after the protocol is published, leading to conflicts and interoperability problems.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC defines how authors should document their IANA Considerations: naming the registries IANA should maintain, specifying what information requesters must provide, and choosing from standard policies (like Expert Review or RFC Required) that determine who can assign new values and under what conditions.
tldr.outcome: RFC 5226 was later superseded by RFC 8126, which provides updated guidance on IANA Considerations.

today: RFC 5226 is a Best Current Practice that was later superseded by RFC 8126, which updates the guidelines for writing IANA Considerations sections in RFCs.

sections.title: Managing Namespaces with IANA
sections.content:
Internet protocols often use namespaces—sets of possible values for a field, such as protocol numbers, option types, or message codes. Once a protocol is deployed, new values need to be assigned for new options or features. To ensure consistent interpretation across all implementations, these assignments must be centrally managed.

For IETF protocols, the Internet Assigned Numbers Authority (IANA) provides this central role. However, IANA needs clear instructions from protocol authors on how to manage each namespace. Without such guidelines, independent extensions might conflict, assigning the same number to different purposes.

This RFC guides authors on how to document IANA Considerations—instructions telling IANA which namespaces to maintain, what information a requester must provide, and what policy governs new assignments. The document also explains the policies themselves and the roles of designated experts who review requests.
sections.eli5: Protocols use numbered lists that grow over time. IANA keeps track of them, but needs clear rules about how to hand out new numbers fairly.

sections.title: Why Manage Namespaces
sections.content:
Three main reasons justify managing a namespace: preventing exhaustion of a limited space, preventing hoarding or waste (such as one party grabbing many desirable names), and avoiding interoperability problems from unreviewed protocol extensions.

The key insight is that new protocol extensions benefit from community review. When a requester publishes a new extension, experts can evaluate whether it fits well with the existing architecture, whether similar functionality already exists, and whether the specification is clear enough for interoperable implementations.

When a namespace is essentially unlimited and poses no interoperability risks, assignments can be made freely without review. In other cases, some form of vetting is appropriate. The RFC discusses different levels of review, from none to full IETF community consensus.
sections.eli5: Numbers are precious. Giving them out wisely prevents wasted numbers, prevents bad extensions, and keeps the protocol healthy.

sections.title: Registration Policies
sections.content:
The RFC defines eight standard registration policies, each suited to different situations:

Private Use: Numbers reserved for local use only, not coordinated with IANA. Useful for site-specific options that do not need global consistency.

Experimental Use: Numbers for experimental testing. IANA does not track which number is used for what.

Hierarchical Allocation: IANA delegates parts of the namespace to others, who can assign further values independently. Examples: DNS names, IP addresses.

First Come First Served: IANA assigns values to anyone who requests them, with minimal review—just a well-formed request with contact information and a brief description.

Expert Review: A designated expert reviews requests to evaluate whether they make sense, fit the architecture, and are clearly specified. The expert acts as a gatekeeper.

Specification Required: Like Expert Review, but additionally requires that the request be documented in a permanent, readily available specification (often an RFC). The Designated Expert evaluates whether the specification is clear and sufficient for interoperability.

RFC Required: Simpler than Specification Required—publication as an RFC (any type) suffices; IANA does not require additional expert review.

IETF Review: New values are assigned only through RFCs shepherded through the IESG with full IETF community review, ensuring the assignment does not harm interoperability.

Standards Action: The strictest policy—only Standards Track RFCs approved by the IESG can request assignments.

Authors should choose the policy that balances openness with protection of the namespace and interoperability.
sections.eli5: Different numbers need different rules: some can be given away freely, others need an expert to check, and the most important ones need full IETF review.

sections.title: Designated Experts and Review
sections.content:
When Expert Review or Specification Required is chosen, IANA relies on a designated expert—typically a subject matter expert appointed by the IESG. The expert is responsible for evaluating requests, coordinating review, and recommending to IANA whether to approve or deny.

The expert may consult technology experts, discuss on public mailing lists, involve working groups, or perform other forms of community review. The expert is expected to respond in a timely manner (normally within a week for simple requests, a few weeks for complex ones) and to defend their decisions to the IETF community.

When there is no documented vetting criteria, the default presumption should be to grant the request unless there is a compelling reason to deny it. Reasons to deny include: scarcity of code points, insufficient documentation to evaluate interoperability, inconsistency with the protocol architecture, or conflict with existing deployed systems.

For some registries, a pool of multiple experts may be appointed, with one as chair. If experts disagree, the chair must provide IANA with a single clear recommendation.
sections.eli5: An expert listens to requests, checks if they make sense, and tells IANA whether to approve them. The expert must be fair and respond quickly.

sections.title: Creating and Maintaining Registries
sections.content:
When an RFC creates a new namespace that IANA will manage, the IANA Considerations section must clearly specify:

Registry name: The exact name that will appear on the IANA website and be referenced in future documents.

Required information: What a requester must provide to request a new value (contact information, description, security considerations if relevant).

Review process: Which of the standard policies applies, or a custom process derived from them.

Format and syntax: What values are allowed (number ranges, string lengths, encoding), how to display them (decimal, hexadecimal, etc.), and what fields to record.

Initial assignments: Any starting values and ranges reserved for special uses (Private Use, Reserved, Unassigned).

When registering new values in an existing registry, documents should clearly identify the namespace, use placeholder notations like TBD1 for numeric values IANA will assign, and provide a summary table showing all requested assignments.

The RFC also covers updating existing registrations, handling after-the-fact assignments that were used without formal registration, and the delicate process of reclaiming unused values for reuse.
sections.eli5: New registries need clear instructions: what's registered, what info is needed, who decides, and how values are formatted. Existing registries can be updated with more guidance.
